newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks drop on fears of stalled settlement.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks drop on fears of stalled settlement.

text.p: The stocks of tobacco companies fell Wednesday on speculation that settlement talks between the tobacco industry, the public health community and state attorneys general would collapse.

Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the nation's No. 1 cigarette maker, was down $1.125 at $45.625 after falling early in the session to $44.50, and RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. was off 87.5 cents at $34.25, both on the New York Stock Exchange.
Tobacco stocks steadied recently as the talks moved from secrecy and out into the open, easing investor fears that the industry would remain clouded with uncertainty.

But Wall Street grew nervous following news that the issue of punitive damages may be unresolved as attorneys general looked set to present the White House with a tobacco settlement proposal this week.
Punitive damages are awarded to punish and deter wrongful behaviour.

Forty states have sued the industry to recoup the costs of treating diseases allegedly caused by smoking, and state officials have said they want a settlement soon or they will go to trial in the first of the lawsuits, in Mississippi starting July 7.

Both sides had hoped to reach an agreement before that trial started, but the talks showed signs of unravelling as industry officials' attitude toward punitive damages and FDA regulation has hardened.

RJR Nabisco Holdings unit R.J. Reynolds on Tuesday struck back at the Federal Trade Commission with a lawsuit that seeks to block the FTC's crackdown on Joe Camel, the tobacco company's controversial marketing symbol.

Also on Tuesday, state attorneys general threatened to walk away from negotiations unless cigarette makers agreed that tobacco would be regulated by the federal Food and Drug Administration, and that they could be punished for wrongful conduct and be held liable for compensatory and punitive damages.

"Since last Thursday, when optimism was high, stocks have performed well. I think it (today's action) is from the fear that there is brinksmanship going on now. There's been some caustic comments lately," said David Adelman, analyst at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Discover.

"Earlier this week, I thought we'd have a deal today. I don't think that's likely, but I still think a deal will come shortly. One thing we have to do is we have to cut through the rhetoric," he said.
